title: Anywhere Reader
user: A blind or low-vision person using a locked-down work, school, kiosk, or game computer who needs to hear the currently visible UI without installing software on that computer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster says accessibility APIs require installation and app support, then asks for a phone-based camera/screen-to-TTS tool that works on any computer.
A map team reports that after a selection, focus moves to the viewport with no audio feedback and requests a screen-reader notification.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests expose the same failure mode: visual state changes remain silent when an accessibility tree is missing or incomplete; this can block a task outright.
current_workaround: Install a screen reader where permitted, use OCR/select-to-speak overlays, ask another person, or abandon the inaccessible workflow.
incumbents_and_gap: NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack, Seeing AI, and HockEye help in their domains, but none offers a deliberately constrained, phone-hosted remote reader that prioritizes a cursor-sized region and never needs credentials on the target machine.
smallest_useful_product: Android app that photographs/streams a selected screen region, performs on-device OCR, reads only changed lines on a push-to-talk gesture, and offers large high-contrast zoom. Non-goals: autonomous clicking, surveillance, cloud recording, or bypassing protected content.
success_measure: In a 10-person pilot, at least 7 complete a three-step task on an unmanaged visual-only app without sighted help in under five minutes.
monetization: one-time — an assistive utility must remain usable without an account or recurring speech quota.
constraints: All OCR/audio must stay on device by default; obtain clear consent before any camera capture; do not defeat DRM, authentication, or employer monitoring controls; accessibility-tree integration is optional only.
why_distinct: It is a constrained remote fallback for inaccessible surfaces, not another general-purpose AI computer agent or cloud vision chatbot.

title: Context Check
user: Dyslexic software engineers and their reviewers who need to catch visually plausible identifier, config-key, and shell-command mistakes before they become production incidents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN participant describes a diligent colleague with a high typo rate causing late catches and production outages; linting and normal review have not solved it.
A product accessibility audit explicitly requests a dyslexia-friendly toggle to reduce reading friction.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 accounts connect dyslexia-related reading friction to work quality; the HN report calls out repeated late defects, making severity higher than ordinary spelling errors.
current_workaround: Rely on spell check, linters, code review, extra tests, or a colleague; these either miss domain tokens or add social friction.
incumbents_and_gap: LanguageTool, cspell, IDE linting, and Grammarly flag spelling, while font toggles only change presentation. They do not compare a change against repository vocabulary and flag confusable, near-duplicate tokens in context.
smallest_useful_product: Local VS Code extension that highlights newly introduced near-matches to existing identifiers, config keys, filenames, and commands; presents a one-line spoken/readable comparison and an explicit dismiss action. Non-goals: AI code generation, performance scoring, or diagnosis.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilot users retain the extension after four weeks and each reports one prevented wrong-key, wrong-file, or wrong-command change.
monetization: free — local-first adoption and accessibility trust matter more than billing; paid team policy/reporting can be evaluated later.
constraints: Never upload source by default; support disabling sensitive paths; suggestions must be explainable and avoid labeling a person or condition.
why_distinct: The unit of help is an explainable repository-context confusion, not generic grammar correction or a dyslexia-font clone.

title: Transcript Tidy
user: People who absorb text better than video or audio, including ADHD users, who need an existing TED or YouTube transcript rendered as a stable, readable document.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user says they absorb text far better than audio/video and asks for a way to obtain and read TED and YouTube transcripts without broken mid-clause copy/paste.
A public-service livestream project is specifying a transcript workflow, showing transcript delivery remains a separately engineered capability rather than a solved viewer experience.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 threads show both individual demand and active implementation work; the individual workaround is sufficiently bad that it requires repeated copying and cleanup.
current_workaround: Open a platform transcript panel, copy fragments into a document, use a downloader, or watch/listen despite the mismatch.
incumbents_and_gap: YouTube, TED, Otter, and transcript downloaders expose text, but commonly leave it fragmented, timestamp-heavy, or tied to an account. A reader-first layer for transcripts already supplied by the source is missing.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that detects an on-page transcript/caption track the user can already access, reflows it into paragraphs with headings and find-in-video links, and exports the user-visible text locally. Non-goals: downloading video, creating transcripts for unavailable works, hosting a transcript library, or summarization.
success_measure: At least 60% of beta users finish reading three imported transcripts and use search or a timestamp jump in the first week.
monetization: one-time — the product is a local reading enhancement, not a transcription compute service.
constraints: Respect site terms and user-visible caption availability; do not redistribute copyrighted transcripts; keep processing local and disclose unsupported sites.
why_distinct: It fixes transcript reading and navigation rather than generating an LLM summary or another caption downloader.

title: Say the Action
user: People with limited keyboard/mouse access who need a small, trustworthy voice-command layer for a few repeatable browser or coding actions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks why an excellent multilingual phone voice interface cannot control their phone and says they would pay for it.
A feature request says people unable to drag, type, or use slow on-screen keyboards face a major barrier to writing code, and asks for speech-based editing.

recurrence: Two independent August 2026 requests, one mobile and one coding, identify input rather than speech transcription as the unmet need; inability to type can fully prevent participation.
current_workaround: Use platform voice access, dictation plus manual correction, bespoke automation, or an on-screen keyboard.
incumbents_and_gap: Voice Access, Voice Control, Talon, and Dragon are broad systems with setup and safety complexity. There is room for a narrow, inspectable command layer that a person can configure for one workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with on-device speech recognition where available, a visible command palette, 10 user-approved DOM actions per site, and a confirmation step for submit/delete/navigation. Non-goals: whole-phone control, arbitrary code execution, hidden background listening, or agentic browsing.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users successfully perform five configured actions by voice with no unintended destructive action over one week.
monetization: one-time — safety and offline operation are more credible without a perpetual voice-data subscription.
constraints: Push-to-talk by default; local command logs; explicit site/action allowlists; confirmation for irreversible actions; never present it as a replacement for platform accessibility tools.
why_distinct: It makes a tiny user-auditable action grammar, not a thin wrapper around a general AI agent.

title: Name Tap
user: Hard-of-hearing people in multilingual group conversations who need to notice when their name or a chosen urgent phrase is spoken.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A hard-of-hearing commenter testing on-device captions says missing their name being called is a major problem and asks for pre-registered name detection with phone/watch vibration.
A chat product separately requests live captions in calls, confirming that caption delivery is still an active accessibility need.

recurrence: Two independent July 2026 caption requests; the HN request states a concrete missed-social-cue harm rather than a generic desire for transcripts.
current_workaround: Watch a live caption wall continuously, ask someone to tap them, or risk missing an address by name.
incumbents_and_gap: Live Caption, Ava, Otter, and conferencing captions transcribe speech, but notification rules are usually absent or cloud/account dependent. The missing layer is a privacy-preserving personal attention cue.
smallest_useful_product: Android app that listens only while the user starts a local live-caption session, matches a small personal phrase list with fuzzy phonetic variants, and sends a distinct vibration/visual cue. Non-goals: recording meetings, speaker identification, voiceprint storage, or emergency dispatch.
success_measure: In a controlled noisy-conversation test, users notice at least 90% of 20 spoken target-name events while reducing continuous screen watching.
monetization: one-time — phrase detection should work offline and remain available during travel or poor connectivity.
constraints: On-device ASR only by default; clear consent screen for conversation capture; no claim of perfect recognition; comply with local recording/consent laws.
why_distinct: It turns captions into a personal haptic attention channel rather than competing as another meeting transcription service.

title: Caption Lanes
user: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people in small in-person groups who need to know which person a live caption belongs to without reading one merged text wall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: SpeechCompass reports a survey of 263 captioning power users where merged speakers were a top issue for 46%, and presents directional captions as the response.
A live-room feature request asks for opt-in translated captions per listener, another 2026 request for captions tailored to each participant.

recurrence: A 263-user survey plus an independent live-room request show captioning demand is not only transcription accuracy; speaker attribution and listener control are recurring usability failures.
current_workaround: Infer speakers from context, manually ask people to identify themselves, use meeting-specific caption products, or read a single mixed transcript.
incumbents_and_gap: Live Transcribe, Ava, Otter, and conferencing captions offer text; SpeechCompass demonstrates direction but requires supported hardware. A lightweight, privacy-respecting two-to-four-person lane UI is still sparse.
smallest_useful_product: Android app for tabletop conversations that renders separate caption lanes and coarse left/center/right direction from the phone microphone array; users can lock a lane color or hide low-confidence text. Non-goals: identity/voiceprint recognition, cloud meeting archives, or forensic audio capture.
success_measure: In a four-person test, participants correctly attribute at least 80% of 30 short utterances while reading captions.
monetization: freemium — a free two-speaker offline mode validates value; a paid multi-device microphone/accessory mode can fund hardware support.
constraints: Communicate direction confidence and microphone limits; process audio locally; obtain consent; do not infer identity or retain raw audio.
why_distinct: It is about visual turn-taking structure, not an LLM transcript, translation wrapper, or generic speaker diarization dashboard.

title: Signal Check
user: Color-blind knowledge workers who need to tell whether a chart, status dashboard, or UI uses color as the only carrier of meaning before they act on it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user says OS and game color-correction options do not cover the full spectrum and asks technical users how they deal with screen color-blindness problems.
A chart-library issue identifies an adjacent red/green categorical pair as colorblind-confusable in the default palette.

recurrence: The HN discussion describes individualized perception and unhelpful blanket filters; the independent chart issue shows the same red/green ambiguity still ships in 2026 tooling.
current_workaround: Turn on an OS filter, ask a colleague, use glasses, or hope that contrast and labels are sufficient.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows/macOS filters, Color Oracle, Stark, and DaltonLens simulate or shift colors. They do not give an end user a quick, page-level explanation of which visual signals are ambiguous and what alternate cue to seek.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that samples the visible page/screenshot, detects repeated color-only legend/status distinctions, simulates selected deficiencies locally, and overlays a plain-language warning with label/shape/position alternatives. Non-goals: medical diagnosis, automatic recoloring of all sites, or design-system replacement.
success_measure: In a 20-chart benchmark, users identify at least 85% of intentionally color-only distinctions after using the overlay, versus their baseline.
monetization: free — broad use improves accessible information; optional team report export can later support a paid tier.
constraints: Simulation is advisory, not a personalized prescription; screenshots may contain sensitive data and must stay local; make overlays keyboard and screen-reader accessible.
why_distinct: It audits meaning in the current task context for the affected reader, rather than applying another global color filter.

title: Comfort Card
user: Players with motion sickness who need a fast, game-specific checklist of visual settings to try before spending an hour becoming nauseated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 33-comment HN thread contains repeated reports of nausea blocking first-person games and requests for head-bob, camera-shake, FOV, motion-blur, and similar controls.
A project independently requests honoring prefers-reduced-motion for decorative animations, showing motion comfort remains an active implementation concern.

recurrence: The HN thread has many independent accounts of avoiding entire game genres and trying inconsistent settings; a separate 2026 issue confirms motion reduction remains omitted by default.
current_workaround: Search scattered forums, toggle settings blindly, edit config files, take medication/breaks, or stop playing.
incumbents_and_gap: Platform reduced-motion settings and game accessibility menus expose some toggles, while PCGamingWiki documents options. Neither produces a simple personal before-play checklist and a portable record of which settings helped a particular player.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that creates a per-game comfort card: symptom triggers, ordered settings to try (head bob, shake, blur, FOV, UI motion), 15-minute check-ins, and a shareable non-identifying card. Non-goals: medical treatment claims, game modding, telemetry collection, or guaranteed compatibility ratings.
success_measure: At least 50% of 30 early users record a session lasting 30 minutes longer than their initial baseline without increasing reported symptoms.
monetization: free — individual comfort data should remain private and portable; no ad model around health-adjacent information.
constraints: Use careful non-medical language; all records local by default; do not imply that settings make a game safe for every user; allow immediate stop guidance.
why_distinct: It is a structured self-advocacy and settings experiment, not a motion-effect clone or an unverified cure app.

title: Calm Page
user: Readers on small e-ink screens or with visual/cognitive reading fatigue who need repeatable large-type, spacing, contrast, and chunking settings for their own DRM-free documents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN buyer seeks current e-reader guidance and commenters repeatedly weigh display contrast, screen size, rendering, and reader software.
An EPUB project opens an accessibility/small-screen comfort epic for compact e-ink readers, including large-type and dyslexia-friendly presets.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 threads frame reading comfort as an unresolved configuration problem across devices, rather than merely choosing an e-reader brand.
current_workaround: Tune each reader separately, convert files in Calibre, install KOReader, or accept poor rendering on smaller devices.
incumbents_and_gap: KOReader, Kindle/Kobo settings, Calibre, and EPUB readers provide controls, but profiles do not travel cleanly across local HTML/EPUB/PDF reading contexts or preserve a reader's tested comfort recipe.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that opens user-supplied DRM-free EPUB/HTML/text, applies named comfort profiles, previews them in an e-ink-style layout, and exports/imports the profile JSON. Non-goals: an ebook store, DRM removal, cloud library, or proprietary device sync.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot readers save and reuse a profile on three separate reading sessions in 14 days.
monetization: one-time — private local documents and a durable profile format are a better fit than a subscription.
constraints: Read files locally; do not process DRM-protected books; support keyboard/screen-reader controls; be transparent that dyslexia fonts are optional preference, not treatment.
why_distinct: The enduring artifact is a portable comfort profile, not another storefront or a generic e-reader clone.

title: Focus Flow Map
user: Keyboard-only, RSI-affected users and the teams supporting them who need to see whether a website's tab order reaches usable controls without hidden jumps or traps.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author of a local computer-vision keyboard-control tool says they built it while suffering RSI and that conventional accessibility APIs fail to cover every app.
A University of Virginia library accessibility audit reports a submission-form keyboard-navigation problem.

recurrence: A personal RSI account and an institutional accessibility audit identify keyboard access as a live usability failure in 2026, with consequences from fatigue to blocked form completion.
current_workaround: Tab through a page by hand, use browser devtools, report the problem with screenshots, or switch to a mouse/assistant.
incumbents_and_gap: axe, Lighthouse, WAVE, and Playwright flag some keyboard rules, but they do not make an end-user-readable focus journey—the actual order, visible target, scroll jump, and dead end—the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that records a user-initiated tab/shift-tab session locally, renders a numbered focus map with element labels and viewport jumps, and exports a reproducible issue packet. Non-goals: automated crawling, a general test suite, or collecting pages remotely.
success_measure: In pilot audits, users attach the exported map to 20 reports and maintainers reproduce at least 70% of reported focus failures on first attempt.
monetization: freemium — local single-page maps should be free; team history and shareable audit workspaces may justify paid hosting.
constraints: Record only on explicit start; redact input values and sensitive URLs; keyboard/screen-reader access to the map itself is mandatory; avoid transmitting site content by default.
why_distinct: It turns the lived keyboard route into evidence, rather than producing another static rule score.

title: Announce Check
user: Small web teams that need to verify the screen-reader announcements of one critical signup, search, or form flow before release.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Guidepup is presented as a screen-reader automation library for testing, evidence that teams need automation around assistive-technology behavior.
Shopware requests full screen-reader testing so all functionality and visual information remain operable/audible to users.

recurrence: Two independent August 2026 efforts show that screen-reader behavior is still tested as a special, labor-intensive concern; the harm is release of an otherwise working flow that is unusable non-visually.
current_workaround: Run manual VoiceOver/NVDA checks late, rely on linting, or adopt a larger automation library and write custom harnesses.
incumbents_and_gap: Guidepup, Playwright, axe, and BrowserStack are capable components. The gap for a small team is a minimal, reviewable expected-announcement transcript test for one business-critical flow.
smallest_useful_product: NPM CLI plus local HTML reporter that drives a short scripted browser flow, captures accessibility-tree/ARIA-live changes, compares them to a checked-in expected transcript, and points to the first divergence. Non-goals: emulating every screen reader, hosted testing SaaS, or WCAG certification.
success_measure: Five pilot teams add one flow each and catch at least one missing label, focus move, or live announcement before deployment in 60 days.
monetization: free — open local fixtures are needed for trust and adoption; a paid managed browser matrix is a later, separate product.
constraints: Be explicit that accessibility trees are not equivalent to screen-reader speech; run against local/authorized URLs; keep fixture data local and avoid logging form values.
why_distinct: It narrows the problem to an approval-friendly announcement contract, not an opaque accessibility score or a full automation framework.

title: Say It Right
user: Dyslexic, low-vision, and language-learning readers who use text-to-speech but need technical terms, names, IPA, and abbreviations pronounced reliably in the material they revisit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creator describes a free dyslexia-oriented TTS reader designed for quickly reading short text sections without selecting text.
A request for IPA pronunciation support in Edge Read Aloud explicitly frames correct pronunciation as an accessibility improvement for blind or visually impaired people.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 TTS requests show basic read-aloud availability is not enough: short-selection flow and pronunciation accuracy still determine whether it is usable.
current_workaround: Listen to a mispronunciation, alter source text temporarily, search a dictionary, or switch voices/readers.
incumbents_and_gap: Edge Read Aloud, Read Aloud, Speechify, Voice Dream, and browser TTS speak text but offer limited portable, source-preserving pronunciation hints tied to a reader's own vocabulary.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with a local per-site pronunciation glossary: select a word/phrase, enter phonetic spelling or a replacement, preview it in the installed voice, and read selected text with highlighted chunks. Non-goals: voice cloning, medical learning claims, cloud text storage, or full-document scraping.
success_measure: At least 70% of beta users save five cues and report that a previously troublesome page is understandable on first listen.
monetization: one-time — personal pronunciation data should stay private and work with installed voices.
constraints: Store cues locally and make export opt-in; respect page permissions; support keyboard operation; do not claim IPA input guarantees a voice engine's exact realization.
why_distinct: It supplies a user-owned pronunciation memory for existing TTS, not another generic text-to-speech front end.
